Functional and morphological evaluation of the meibomian glands and ocular 
surface assessment at high altitude
Zhouyu Li, Wenjuan Wan, Yan Ji, Shijie Zheng, Ke Hu
Access this article online
Website:

Quick Response Code:
Purpose: To compare the function and morphology of the meibomian glands and the ocular surface of 
individuals from highland and lowland. Methods: This was a randomized controlled trial. The study 
was performed with 104 individuals  (51 individuals from the highland and 53 individuals from the 
lowland). Detailed eye examinations comprising tear meniscus height, lipid layer grading, non‑invasive 
Keratograph tear breakup time  (NIKBUT), and scoring of the meibomian glands from the upper and 
lower eyelids of the individuals were performed by Keratograph  5M  (OCULUS, Wetzlar, Germany). 
Symptoms related to dry eye disease were assessed using the Ocular Surface Disease Index  (OSDI). 
Results: In the highland group, tear meniscus height was lower (P = 0.024), lipid layer grade, as well as 
all the meiboscores were higher (P < 0.05) than that in the lowland group. The OSDI (P = 0.018) and the 
percentage of dry eye disease were also higher as compared to that of the lowland group (P = 0.032). The 
first NIKBUT and average NIKBUT did not differ significantly between groups. The frequency of plugged 
meibomian gland orifices was greater in the lowland group compared to the highland group (P = 0.036). 
Conclusion: It was observed that dry eye disease was more common in the highland group. The 
morphological changes of meibomian gland dropout were significant in highlanders as demonstrated 
objectively with Keratograph 5M. Our study may raise a concern for environmental influences on ocular 
surface changes.
Key words: Dry eye disease, high altitude, meibomian glands, ocular surface

Meibomian glands are sebaceous glands that prevent 
evaporation by secreting tear film lipids. These glands keep the 
ocular surface healthy. Meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD) 
results in lipid layer abnormalities and tear film instability. It 
is the primary cause of evaporative dry eye disease, and hence, 
has recently attracted attention as a cause of ocular discomfort. 
High altitude, characterized by hypobaric hypoxia, low 
temperature, and intensive ultraviolet radiation, is associated 
with physiological and some pathological changes[1‑3] and has 
potentially undesired ophthalmic effects.[4] Native Tibetans, 
especially the nomadic people who perform daily outdoor 
activities, spend a considerable amount of time outside 
during long daylight hours (usually 7–9 h/d) without any eye 
protection. This may change the structure and/or function of the 
meibomian glands, leading to harmful effects. The prevalence 
of dry eye disease is higher in high‑altitude residents than in 
low‑altitude residents.[5] However, MGD, the most common 
cause of dry eye disease, and the morphology of the meibomian 
glands have not been investigated. The ocular analyzer, the 
Keratograph  5M  (OCULUS, Wetzlar, Germany), enables 
non‑invasive visualization, i.e. quantifies gland dropouts 
and evaluates ocular surface function objectively. This study 
aimed to compare the morphological and functional changes 
in the meibomian glands and other eye surface differences 
between individuals residing at high and low altitudes using 
the Keratograph 5M.
Methods
The protocol of this study was approved by the Ethics

Committee of Chongqing Medical University Hospital and 
Zhag’yab People's Hospital. Figure 1 showed the location of 
Zhag’yab County and Chongqing City. The nature of the study 
and the procedures were performed as per the Declaration 
of Helsinki. The procedures were explained fully to all the 
participants, and their informed consent was obtained before 
beginning the examinations. At Zhag’yab, all procedures were 
conducted in the local language by a trained physician and a 
trained nurse.
Participants
The study was undertaken between August 2019 and 
September 2019 with two groups of individuals  –  the 
highland group [the study group with 51 patients residing 
at Zhag’yab County  (3700  m above sea level)] and the 
lowland group [the control group with 53 patients residing

in both groups were selected randomly from the patients 
attending the outpatient departments of the two hospitals. 
All participants were born, raised, and resided in the study 
area for over ten years. Subjects with acute ocular infection, 
extensive corneal or conjunctival pathology, contact lens 
users, and those with a history of any ocular surgery or 
systemic autoimmune or mucocutaneous disease were 
excluded from the study. Smokers and alcoholics were 
also excluded. Additionally, the selected subjects had not 
received any antibiotics, corticosteroids, or non‑steroidal 
anti‑inflammatory drugs in the last six months. In addition, 
fasting blood glucose of participants has been tested in 
our study, which did not revealed any high blood glucose 
history.
Tear film metrics
Tear film metrics were assessed with the Oculus 
Keratograph 5M (OCULUS Inc., Germany) to evaluate tear 
meniscus height  (TMH) and non‑invasive Keratograph 
tear breakup time (NIKBUT, including NIKBUT‑first and 
NIKBUT‑average) from both eyes of each subject. The mean 
value of three consecutive measurements was taken for each 
corneal parameter, and the time interval between consecutive 
measurements was at least 60 s.
A video was recorded for 5–8 s under natural blink 
conditions to measure the lipid layer. The thickness of the 
lipid layer was graded into three levels based on the structural 
clarity and color richness: thin (level 1), normal (level 2), and 
thick (level 3). A thin lipid layer is fuzzy and grayish. A normal 
lipid layer is clear, with a rich color. A thick lipid layer is very 
clear, with an extremely rich color.[6]
OSDI evaluation
The Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) questionnaire was 
completed for each subject to assess subjective symptoms.[7] 
The OSDI is a frequency‑based questionnaire that contains 
three ocular symptom questions, six vision‑related function 
questions, and three environmental trigger questions.
Meibomian gland assessment
Following eyelid eversion, infrared images of the meibomian 
glands were captured via the Keratograph 5M (OCULUS Inc., 
Germany). Then, the Meibo‑Scan Program was used to confirm 
the meibomian gland loss, documenting the following scores 
as appropriate – 0: no absence; 1: <1/3 of glands absent; 2: >1/3 
but <2/3 of glands absent; and 3: >2/3 glands absent.[8] The 
meiboscore values of the lower, upper, and total (upper and 
lower) eyelids were calculated for each eye [Fig. 2]. Additionally,

lid margins for plugged orifices of meibomian glands were 
scored as 0 (absent) or 1 (present)[9] in each eyelid [Fig. 3].
Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were performed in SPSS 22.0 (SPSS Inc., 
Chicago, IL, USA). Data from the left eye were included in the 
statistical analysis. If the left eye was excluded from the study, 
data from the right eye were used. T‑test, Chi‑squared test, 
and Mann–Whitney U‑test were used to compare variables 
between the groups. The statistically significant threshold was 
considered at P < 0.05.
Results
The mean age of the subjects was 56.29  ±  21.24  (range, 
16–92), and the male‑to‑female ratio was 22:29 in the 
highland group, neither of sex ratio and age was significantly 
different from the lowland group (P = 0.230 and P = 0.477, 
respectively) [Table 1].
Ocular surface tests revealed that OSDI and the mean 
lipid layer score were significantly higher in the highland 
group than that in the lowland group (P = 0.018 and P < 0.001, 
respectively). While the mean value of TMH in the highland 
group was lower than that in the lowland group (P = 0.024). 
The NIKBUT‑first values and the NIKBUT‑average values 
did not differ significantly between the highland and lowland 
groups. Based on the criteria of the Asia Dry Eye Society report, 
subjects with an Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI total 
score) ≥13 and a strict tear breakup time ≤5 s were diagnosed 
as DED.[10] The percentage of DED in the highland group was

Abnormalities in the lid margins were observed more 
frequently in the lowland group, recorded as 35.85% for 
plugged meibomian gland orifices (P = 0.036). Evaluation of 
the meibomian gland dropout revealed by upper, lower, and 
total (upper and lower) meiboscore values was significantly 
higher in the highland group than that in the lowland 
group (P = 0.021, P = 0.014, and P = 0.048, respectively) [Table 2].
Discussion
According to the results of the present study, the percentage 
of DED among the highland group was higher which was 
accordance with the results of the study conducted at high altitude 
in a Himalayan region in India (20% compared to 9% at low 
altitude).[5] DED is a multifactorial disease,[10] with atmospheric 
pressure and air pollution being the most influential risk factors.[11] 
Air pollution and changed atmospheric pressure are associated 
with increased symptoms and diagnosis of DED.[12,13] The decline 
in the atmospheric pressure and humidity associated with high 
altitudes increases the rate of evaporation,[14,15] which further 
contributed to the increased percentage of dry eye disease in 
the highland group. Besides, we hypothesize that outdoor ozone 
pollution probably contributed to the elevated percentage of dry 
eye disease in the highland group. It was revealed that the ozone 
level was within the standard range in Chongqing City (49.36 
μg/m3), although it was higher in Zhag’yab County, Tibet (67.55 
μg/m3) (CMDC, personal communication). Long‑term contact 
with ozone can break down the corneal‑epithelial integrity and 
reduce mucin‑secreting cells.[16,17] Moreover, people from the 
highland who perform pasturing have increased exposure to 
UV light due to the thin air and cloud cover, thereby intensifying 
the inflammation and oxidative stress on the ocular surface.[15,16] 
Chronic inflammation and oxidative stress at the ocular surface 
may led to damage of the transmembrane‑bound mucins 
extending from microvilli or microplicae to stabilize the tear 
film.[18,19] It has been demonstrated that the significance of these 
biochemical (mucin) and biophysical (microvilli/microplicae) 
attributes to corneal epithelial cell wettability, which is directly 
related to tear film stability.[20] Thus, DED was detected more 
frequently in highlanders, possibly on account of the synthetic

effect of these important risk factors varying with altitude. The 
finding that a high percentage of women had dry eye disease is 
consistent with earlier studies conducted.[5,21,22]
DED was classified as two predominant and non‑mutually 
exclusive categories: 1) aqueous deficient dry eye and 2) evaporative 
dry eye, with evaporative dry eye being more common.[7] MGD 
constitutes the primary cause of evaporative‑type DED. The 
meibomian glands, important components of the lacrimal 
functional unit,[7] are one of the chief determinants of the health of 
the ocular surface.[23] To date, MGD and the changes in meibomian 
gland morphology have not been investigated in highlands.
We found a greater degree of meibomian gland dropout 
in the highland group than the lowland group. By integrating 
environmental data from China Meteorological Data Service 
Center (CMDC) (http://data.cma.cn/), it was found that Zhag’yab 
had longer sunshine hours, more intense ultraviolet rays, and 
a drier environment annually compared to Chongqing; these 
factors cause senile in the highland group, including that of the 
visual organs.[24] When senescence occurs in human eyelids, the 
meibomian glands begin to atrophy, and dropout occurs more 
frequently due to depletion of the meibocyte stem cells.[25] Due 
to the increased frequency of meibomian gland dropout, the 
quantity and quality of the secretion decrease. This leads to an 
unstable lipid layer of the tear film, causing rapid evaporation 
of the underlying aqueous layer.[26]
Intuitively, one may conclude that the meibomian gland 
dropout may decrease the supply of lipids, leading to the 
destruction of the lipid layer integrity, since the meibomian 
gland acinar epithelial cells secrete lipids  (meibum) into 
tears, forming a superficial lipid layer that stabilizes the tear 
film layer.[27] However, the lipid layer score was higher in the 
highland group, with richer color and more homogeneous 
distribution. This may be due to hypoxia and low humidity 
stress. It was showed that the average oxygen level in Chongqing 
City was 20.53%, while in Zhag’yab was 15.09% (CMDC, 
personal communication). Additionally, the average humidity 
during the study period was 63.97% in the highland and 55.30% 
in the lowland (CMDC, personal communication). Meibomian 
glands can respond dynamically to environmental stress.[25] 
The meibomian gland acinar epithelial cells’ production and 
release of lipids are different from that in other lipid‑producing 
cells.[27] Low O2 level does not alter the number of meibomian 
glands; instead, it benefits their function.[28] Moreover, animal 
experiments have shown that meibocytes proliferate more 
in a desiccating environment.[25] Both these factors are likely 
to increase meibum synthesis to maintain the lipid layer 
balance.[28] These facts provide evidence to potentially explain 
the difference in the lipid layer between the two groups.
The tear meniscus height (TMH) can be used to indirectly 
assess the tear film volume. The average TMH in a healthy 
population, measured with the Keratograph  5M, has 
been reported to be 0.27 mm; a cutoff value of 0.20 mm is 
recommended to diagnose abnormal tear volume.[29] Compared 
to these measurements, the average TMH for subjects in this 
study was within a healthy range (above 0.21mm). When 
comparing the average values, TMH was lower in the highland 
group, which might have been due to low humidity and low 
atmospheric pressure (60 kPa in the highland vs 98 kPa in the 
lowland) associated with high altitudes, where evaporative 
water loss is high.[14,15] Besides, evaporative experiments in vitro 
have indicated that the tear film lipid layer reduces evaporation 
partially. However, this reduction is minuscule and cannot 
prevent evaporative dry eyes.[30] These results suggested that 
highland patients seem to be related with evaporative dry eyes.
Interestingly, the plugged meibomian gland orifice was found 
to be more frequent in the lowland group than in the highland one.

A past study has found geographical diversification of ocular surface 
microbiota as well as functional differences in normal eyes.[31] Apart 
from this, certain difference was found between the microbiota 
composition of the ocular surface of MGD patients and the 
composition of healthy people.[22,32,33] Therefore, it is speculated that 
differences in ocular microbiota composition may alter the activity 
of bacterial lipase, resulting in the production of stagnant lipids in 
individuals from lowlands,[34] which leads to the obstruction of the 
meibomian gland orifices.[35] The link between ocular microbiota 
composition and bacterial lipase activity requires further evaluation.
Conclusion
The results of the present study recorded the changes in the 
meibomian gland in highlanders using an objective tool. 
However, the sample size of the study was small and, therefore, 
a comparative future work with a larger study population

could provide further information regarding the risk factors for 
MGD in evaporative DED patients exposed to high altitudes. In 
addition to the above findings, the results of the dry eye tests 
were in favor of the evaporative type in DED patients from 
the highlands. However, Keratograph 5M is not applicable for 
the detection of tear osmolarity and lacrimal secretion testing. 
Therefore, further comprehensive tests are warranted to further 
investigate the subtype classification of DED, which would offer 
greater information regarding which type of DED was affected 
further significantly by the change in altitude. This DED type 
could be only the evaporative type or a mixed type. Overall, the 
result data from the present study raises a concern regarding 
the environmental influences on ocular surface changes.
